summary:
North Chungcheong Province stands under the national framework of South Korea, where gender identity and gender expression are not criminalised in civilian life and consensual same-sex conduct between adults is legal. The surviving criminal provision is Military Criminal Act article 92-6, which punishes consensual same-sex conduct among military personnel with up to two years' imprisonment; the Constitutional Court upheld it in 2023. Enforcement has been punitive and targeted. In 2017 the military ran what Amnesty International described as a gay witch hunt, criminally charging 32 personnel, and a gay soldier received a six-month prison sentence for consensual sex. Transgender people are excluded from military service altogether.

This province is the location of the gravest documented harm to a transgender service member in South Korea. Staff Sergeant Byun Hui-su, the country's first openly transgender soldier, was found dead at her home in Cheongju on 3 March 2021, aged 23. She had been compulsorily discharged in early 2020 after a military panel classified the effects of her gender-affirming surgery as a physical or mental handicap, and her challenge to that discharge was rejected in July 2020. Her death triggered national debate on the treatment of transgender troops. The Daejeon District Court later ruled the discharge unjust and reinstated her posthumously on 7 October 2021, and in March 2024 the Ministry of National Defence recognised her death as in the line of duty.

Legal gender recognition is available in South Korea and the surgical precondition is falling away. On 8 May 2024 a South Korean court held that requiring sex-reassignment surgery as a condition of changing legal sex status violates physical integrity, ruling for five plaintiffs assigned male at birth who had undergone years of hormone therapy, and held that outdated judicial guidelines cannot ground dismissals. On 24 November 2022 the Supreme Court ruled en banc that transgender individuals who are unmarried may have their gender legally recognised even when they have minor children, overturning an 11-year-old precedent; a 2011 Supreme Court ruling had required persons seeking gender-affirming care to be over 20, single and without children.

National law does not recognise same-sex marriage or civil unions, and same-sex couples cannot adopt children jointly. The 2024 Constitutional Court ruling on same-sex partners' healthcare rights is the main advance in that area. No comprehensive anti-discrimination law covers sexual orientation or gender identity: an anti-discrimination bill has been introduced eight times since 2007, the June 2020 draft included gender-identity provisions, and prosecutors and activists called for its passage after Byun Hee-soo's death. LGBTI organisations can register, though an NGO won registration litigation at the Seoul Metropolitan Court in March 2017 and the government appealed onward, part of what Human Rights Watch described as years of bureaucratic obstruction.

Restroom access is a documented problem in both judicial and school settings. On 2 July 2024 the Seoul Central District Court ruled final, with no appeal available, that police advice telling a transgender plaintiff undergoing gender correction to avoid public restrooms infringed personal rights, ordering symbolic compensation of 300,000 won against the state. Research from the youth LGBTQ+ centre DDing Dong, presented on 20 March 2024, shows transgender teenagers avoid school restrooms for fear of being outed; a 16-year-old trans girl at a boys' school reported holding it in and leaving school early, and researchers called for legal and institutional reform of school environments.

Healthcare carries an official blind spot identified from within the state itself. In November 2023 the National Human Rights Commission of Korea identified a transgender blind spot in hospitalisation after the Ministry of Health and Welfare rejected a request to draft hospitalisation guidelines for transgender patients, reasoning that accommodating diverse circumstances is difficult.

Documented violence concentrates at public events. In Incheon a Pride event ended in violence when roughly 1,000 Christian protestors attacked participants, after which organisers filed charges against pastors and accused police of inaction; at Busan's 2018 Pride some 2,000 police were deployed to protect 15,000 attendees from violent anti-gay protesters. During the May 2020 Itaewon COVID-19 cluster, contact tracing outed LGBTQ people, doxing and online harassment rose, and a trans-male bartender told NBC News he felt threatened walking on the street in the absence of a nondiscrimination bill.

Following Byun Hee-soo's death, the National Human Rights Commission honoured her and national pressure for protection grew, but no new law at provincial level followed; the protection gap is national, not local.
tangentialFactors:
The 2021 incident in Cheongju sits within a national pattern rather than a provincial one. Hate-motivated disruption of Pride events has been recorded in several large South Korean cities, from the attack by about 1,000 protestors in Incheon to the deployment of 2,000 officers against anti-gay protesters at Busan's 2018 Pride, indicating that counter-protest risk attaches to public LGBTQ+ events across the country.

Survey evidence points to a pervasive discrimination burden rather than a regional one. A 2014 finding recorded that 54% of LGBTQ Korean youths were harassed by classmates; 16.1% of outed LGBTQ people were recommended conversion therapy, with 65.4% reporting harm and 94% psychological trauma; a 2018 study found 51.5% of transgender adults had faced harsh discrimination in the preceding year.

A peer-reviewed nationwide survey published on 27 June 2025 in Epidemiology and Health, covering 585 transgender and non-binary young adults, mapped milestones and stigmatisation across life stages and documented discrimination at school, work and in transition-related care. Human Rights Watch's World Report 2025 describes an overall relatively positive record on free media and civil society alongside persistent documented discrimination against LGBT people.
localsOnly:
Transgender residents of North Chungcheong Province are barred from military service under national policy and, if they serve, face article 92-6 exposure; the discharge of Staff Sergeant Byun Hui-su and the rejection of her challenge in July 2020 show how the military classification of gender-affirming care as a handicap has been applied to serving personnel.

Residents seeking legal gender recognition can do so without proving sex-reassignment surgery after the 8 May 2024 ruling, and an unmarried transgender parent may obtain recognition after the Supreme Court's en banc decision of 24 November 2022. The earlier 2011 conditions of age, marital status and childlessness no longer govern.

Same-sex couples living in the province cannot marry, enter a civil union or adopt jointly, and there is no anti-discrimination statute to invoke on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity. LGBTI groups can register as organisations, but the registration history has been contested in court and on appeal since March 2017.

Transgender patients admitted to hospitals in the province have no dedicated national hospitalisation guidelines, following the Ministry of Health and Welfare's refusal in November 2023 to draft them; the National Human Rights Commission of Korea has flagged this as a transgender blind spot. Transgender students in local schools continue to avoid shared restrooms, and residents have a documented record of being outed through public-health contact tracing.
outOfScopeNotes:
The inventory contains no North Chungcheong-specific statute, ordinance, enforcement record, Pride event, shelter or clinic data. Provincial conditions in this record are inferred from national law and from the single Cheongju incident; whether North Chungcheong has adopted any local nondiscrimination or school-safety measure is not sourced here.

Whether an anti-discrimination bill has been enacted since the eighth introduction in 2020 is unresolved in this inventory; the latest sourced position is that none had passed and that activists continued to call for one in 2021.

The reporting on Byun Hee-soo's death gives 3 March 2021 as the date she was found dead, following a counsellor raising the alarm on 28 February; the inventory does not resolve the discrepancy between those dates beyond stating both. Facility-level detail for Cheongju and the rest of the province, including hospital practice and school-district policy, is not sourced.
